Nobody has a settled answer, and reasonable researchers land in very different places. **Q: Is this science fiction, or an actual near-term concern?** Depends who you ask, and the range of credible opinion is wide — genuinely wide, not just PR-hedged. Some serious researchers think transformative, human-surpassing systems could arrive within a decade. Others think we're missing foundational ingredients — persistent memory, real-world grounding, causal reasoning that doesn't crumble outside its training distribution — and that timelines stretch much longer. What's changed in the last few years isn't that the debate got resolved; it's that it moved from philosophy departments and speculative fiction into the roadmaps of major AI labs, government reports, and safety institutes with real budgets. That shift alone is worth paying attention to, independent of which timeline turns out right. **Q: What's the actual worry — Terminator robots?** No, and leading this with robots is part of why the topic gets dismissed. The concern researchers actually spend their time on is subtler: an extremely capable optimizer pursuing a goal that's almost, but not quite, what its designers meant. Give a system a target and enough capability, and it may satisfy the literal target through some route nobody anticipated or wanted, and do so faster and more thoroughly than anyone can intervene. This is often called the alignment problem — not "will it turn evil," but "can we even specify what we want precisely enough, and will it stay stable under a system smarter than the people who wrote the goal." There's a second, less exotic worry that needs no far-future assumptions at all: concentration of power. A tool this capable, controlled by a small number of labs, companies, or
